paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אַבְרָהָ֗ם אֶל־עַבְדּוֹ֙ זְקַ֣ן בֵּית֔וֹ הַמֹּשֵׁ֖ל בְּכָל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֑וֹ שִֽׂים־נָ֥א יָדְךָ֖ תַּ֥חַת יְרֵכִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Avraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, Put, I pray you, your hand under my thigh,

paragraphs.commentary:
*Sim-na yadkha tachat yereki* — *put, please, your hand under my thigh* — is the chapter's first lexical-keystone moment. The gesture is the formal-juridical ANE oath-by-the-thigh; the standard ASV / KJV / NRSV / NJPS translations all preserve the literal *thigh*, and the WoH translation follows.

The verb *yarekh* (יָרֵךְ) means *thigh* in the strict anatomical sense (Gen 32:26 of Ya'aqov's wrestling-injury; Num 5:21 of the *sotah*'s thigh), but in the legal-formulaic register of the two oath-passages it is widely read as a euphemism for the *genital area* — the seat of generative power, the source of the patriarchal seed-line whose continuation the oath is meant to secure. The reading is the modern critical consensus (Sarna *JPS* p. 163; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* p. 384; Wenham *WBC* p. 141; Hamilton *NICOT* pp. 139-140; Alter p. 117; Speiser *AB* p. 178). Rashi at Gen 24:2 cites *Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer* 16 and reads the gesture as touching the circumcised member — *because that is the first commandment that came upon him* — connecting the oath to the *brit milah* covenantal-organ. The Hebrew euphemism is preserved in translation rather than disambiguated in the text.

The gesture's only other HB occurrence is Gen 47:29, where Ya'aqov commissions Yosef for the burial-oath using identical language (*sim-na yadkha tachat yereki*) paired with the *chesed v-emet* formula. The two HB instances share a structural pattern: a patriarchal father-figure at the end of his active life commissions an authorized agent on a matter the principal cannot personally accomplish — Avraham cannot travel to Aram-Naharaim; Ya'aqov cannot personally choose his burial-site in Kena'an. Malul 1985 (*VT* 35) develops the genital-touch reading and proposes the parallel to the *pachad Yitzchaq* (*Thigh of Yitzchaq*) at Gen 31:42, 53; Hill 1967 (*JBL* 86) treats the gesture in its formal-juridical register.

The ANE-comparative context: oath-on-fertility-symbol is widespread in the Mesopotamian, Hittite, Ugaritic, and Egyptian corpora — oaths by the cult-statue's genitals, by the king's sceptre, by the bull's testicles — but the specific gesture of *touching another person's genital area to swear an oath* is rare in the extant ANE texts. The two HB occurrences are the principal documentary attestation; the gesture's logic is comprehensible within the wider ANE pattern but its specific form is editorially distinctive to the patriarchal-narrative tradition.

paragraphs.text: וְאַשְׁבִּ֣יעֲךָ֔ בַּֽיהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וֵֽאלֹהֵ֖י הָאָ֑רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא־תִקַּ֤ח אִשָּׁה֙ לִבְנִ֔י מִבְּנוֹת֙ הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י יוֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: and I will make you swear by YHWH, the Elohim of the heavens and the Elohim of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Kena'ani, among whom I dwell;

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse contains the first occurrence in the Hebrew Bible of the formula *YHWH Elohei ha-shamayim v-Elohei ha-aretz* — *YHWH, the Elohim of the heavens and the Elohim of the earth* — and the first occurrence of the bare *Elohei ha-shamayim* construction. The doubled cosmographic-binitarian construct (heavens + earth under a single divine sovereignty) is the most-developed form of the formula in the patriarchal narratives; the bare *Elohei ha-shamayim* recurs at v 7 in Avraham's continued commissioning-speech, and then disappears from Genesis.

Across the rest of the canonical Hebrew Bible, the *Elohei ha-shamayim* phrase is concentrated in post-exilic and Persian-period literature: Jonah 1:9, Ezra 1:2, 5:11-12, 6:9-10, 7:12-23, Neh 1:4-5, 2:4-20, Dan 2:18-44, Ps 136:26. The cross-corpus distribution generates a well-known source-critical question. **Westermann** (*Genesis 12-36* pp. 384-385) and **Hamilton** (*NICOT* pp. 138-139) read the Gen 24 occurrence as a Persian-period stock-phrase imported into the patriarchal narrative — evidence of late composition for the chapter as a whole. **Sarna** (*JPS* p. 164) reads it as a context-sensitive diplomatic-foreign-context idiom: Avraham is commissioning a journey into a foreign land (Aram-Naharaim) where the local cult is not YHWHistic, and the formula establishes YHWH's universal sovereignty in cosmographic-binitarian terms a foreign audience would recognize. The formula is concentrated in the foreign-context speeches (vv 3, 7), not in the narrative-prose, which supports the diplomatic-context reading.

The WoH translation preserves the article-bearing construct per established Elohim-policy: *the Elohim of the heavens and the Elohim of the earth* (rather than ASV's *the God of heaven and the God of earth*). The lens-relevant late-period-vs.-diplomatic-context question is held in this commentary; the translated text reads as standard scholarly English.

i18n.en: YHWH, the Elohim of the heavens, who took me from my father's house, and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me, and who swore to me, saying, To your seed I will give this land — he will send his messenger before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.

paragraphs.commentary: The bare *Elohei ha-shamayim* recurs without the *v-Elohei ha-aretz* second member, paired with an explicit thematic cross-reference to Gen 12:1-4 (*lekh-lekha*): *YHWH ... asher l'qachani mi-beit avi u-me-eretz moladti* — *YHWH, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred*. The cross-reference is editorial-thematic rather than lexical (the *lekh-lekha* lexeme itself is not present at v 7), so the *lekh-lekha* glossary entry is not applied; the Abraham-from-Ur formula and the seed-land promise (*l-zarakha eten et-ha-aretz ha-zot*) are covered by *zera-eretz-promise*. The verse rehearses the chapter's diplomatic-context register: YHWH is named in his cosmographic-binitarian sovereignty (heavens) and his patriarchal-history specificity (the one who took Avraham from Aram) — the formula functioning as both universal-sovereignty claim and historical-anchoring.

paragraphs.text: וְאִם־לֹ֨א תֹאבֶ֤ה הָֽאִשָּׁה֙ לָלֶ֣כֶת אַחֲרֶ֔יךָ וְנִקִּ֕יתָ מִשְּׁבֻעָתִ֖י זֹ֑את רַ֣ק אֶת־בְּנִ֔י לֹ֥א תָשֵׁ֖ב שָֽׁמָּה׃

i18n.en: And if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you shall be clear from this oath of mine; only you shall not bring my son back there.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֤שֶׂם הָעֶ֙בֶד֙ אֶת־יָד֔וֹ תַּ֛חַת יֶ֥רֶךְ אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֲדֹנָ֑יו וַיִּשָּׁ֣בַֽע ל֔וֹ עַל־הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּֽה׃

i18n.en: And the servant put his hand under the thigh of Avraham his master, and swore to him concerning this matter.

paragraphs.commentary: The servant executes the oath-gesture commanded at v 2 — same lexeme, same euphemistic register; see the v 2 commentary.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֣ח הָ֠עֶבֶד עֲשָׂרָ֨ה גְמַלִּ֜ים מִגְּמַלֵּ֤י אֲדֹנָיו֙ וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ וְכָל־ט֥וּב אֲדֹנָ֖יו בְּיָד֑וֹ וַיָּ֗קָם וַיֵּ֛לֶךְ אֶל־אֲרַ֥ם נַֽהֲרַ֖יִם אֶל־עִ֥יר נָחֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed, having all goodly things of his master's in his hand. And he arose, and went to Aram-Naharayim, to the city of Nachor.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּבְרֵ֧ךְ הַגְּמַלִּ֛ים מִח֥וּץ לָעִ֖יר אֶל־בְּאֵ֣ר הַמָּ֑יִם לְעֵ֣ת עֶ֔רֶב לְעֵ֖ת צֵ֥את הַשֹּׁאֲבֹֽת׃

i18n.en: And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time when women go out to draw water.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמַ֓ר ׀ יְהוָ֗ה אֱלֹהֵי֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י אַבְרָהָ֔ם הַקְרֵה־נָ֥א לְפָנַ֖י הַיּ֑וֹם וַעֲשֵׂה־חֶ֕סֶד עִ֖ם אֲדֹנִ֥י אַבְרָהָֽם׃

i18n.en: And he said, YHWH, the Elohim of my master Avraham, grant me good speed, I pray you, this day, and show chesed to my master Avraham.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The first direct prayer of a non-patriarch in the Hebrew Bible** (Sarna *JPS* p. 165). The servant addresses YHWH directly with the four-element prose-prayer structure that **Greenberg** (*Biblical Prose Prayer* 1983 pp. 7-12) reads as foundational: (i) divine address-formula (*YHWH*); (ii) historical-anchoring phrase (*Elohei adoni Avraham*); (iii) petition (*haqreh-na lefanai ha-yom* — *grant me good speed this day*); (iv) appeal to divine virtue (*va-aseh-chesed im adoni Avraham* — *show chesed to my master Avraham*). Prior to this verse, direct divine address in Genesis is concentrated in patriarchal figures (Avraham at 15:2-3, 8; 17:18; 18:23-32) and in YHWH-initiated dialogue. The verse authorizes prayer-as-direct-address for figures outside the patriarchal-prophetic circle, establishing the *general-servant prayer-access* pattern standard in the later HB. **Miller** *They Cried to the Lord* 1994 pp. 100-105 extends the analysis to the sign-seeking sub-structure at vv 13-14.

The lexeme *chesed* is preserved untranslated per established WoH policy on theologically-loaded terms with no single English equivalent (parallel to *nefesh*, *Elohim*, *YHWH*); the apparatus carries the philological background. The full *chesed v-emet* virtue-pair appears at vv 27 and 49; see the entry *chesed-v-emet-steadfast-love-and-truth*.

The servant prays not as an individual-religious-subject but as an authorized-agent of Avraham's covenantal relation: he names YHWH as *Elohei adoni Avraham* (not as his own deity), petitions for *chesed im adoni Avraham*, and reads the test-result (v 14b) as *kI-asita chesed im-adoni*. The pattern is the **agent-prayer** sub-genre, recurring at Gen 32:10-13 (Ya'aqov at the Jabbok), Exod 32:11-14 and Num 14:13-19 (Moses), 1 Sam 12:23 (Samuel).

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּ֛ה אָנֹכִ֥י נִצָּ֖ב עַל־עֵ֣ין הַמָּ֑יִם וּבְנוֹת֙ אַנְשֵׁ֣י הָעִ֔יר יֹצְאֹ֖ת לִשְׁאֹ֥ב מָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: Behold, I am standing by the spring of water; and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֣ה הַֽנַּעֲרָ֗ אֲשֶׁ֨ר אֹמַ֤ר אֵלֶ֙יהָ֙ הַטִּי־נָ֤א כַדֵּךְ֙ וְאֶשְׁתֶּ֔ה וְאָמְרָ֣ה שְׁתֵ֔ה וְגַם־גְּמַלֶּ֖יךָ אַשְׁקֶ֑ה אֹתָ֤הּ הֹכַ֙חְתָּ֙ לְעַבְדְּךָ֣ לְיִצְחָ֔ק וּבָ֣הּ אֵדַ֔ע כִּי־עָשִׂ֥יתָ חֶ֖סֶד עִם־אֲדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: Let it come to pass that the young woman to whom I shall say, Let down your jar, I pray you, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give your camels drink also — let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant, for Yitzchaq; and by this I shall know that you have shown chesed to my master.

paragraphs.commentary: The conditional structure *v-haya ha-na'arah asher omar eleha ... v-amrah ... otah hokhachta l-avdekha* is the chapter's **divinatory sign-test**: a future-conditional whose fulfillment will be read as direct divine designation. The sub-genre recurs in modified form at **Judg 6:36-40** (Gideon's fleece-test — the canonical HB sign-seeking pericope) and at **1 Sam 14:8-10** (Jonathan's omen at Michmash). Gen 24:14 is the inaugural instance — earlier in the canonical sequence and providing the template for the later instances. The test's lexical core is the verb *hokhicha* (hiphil of y-k-ch — *to determine, designate, appoint*) which becomes the technical-juridical term for divine designation in the chapter (recurring at v 44 in the recitation-block).

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי־ה֗וּא טֶרֶם֮ כִּלָּ֣ה לְדַבֵּר֒ וְהִנֵּ֧ה רִבְקָ֣ה יֹצֵ֗את אֲשֶׁ֤ר יֻלְּדָה֙ לִבְתוּאֵ֣ל בֶּן־מִלְכָּ֔ה אֵ֥שֶׁת נָח֖וֹר אֲחִ֣י אַבְרָהָ֑ם וְכַדָּ֖הּ עַל־שִׁכְמָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, before he had finished speaking, that behold, Rivkah came out, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milkah, the wife of Nachor, Avraham's brother, with her jar upon her shoulder.

paragraphs.text: וְהַֽנַּעֲרָ֗ טֹבַ֤ת מַרְאֶה֙ מְאֹ֔ד בְּתוּלָ֕ה וְאִ֖ישׁ לֹ֣א יְדָעָ֑הּ וַתֵּ֣רֶד הָעַ֔יְנָה וַתְּמַלֵּ֥א כַדָּ֖הּ וַתָּֽעַל׃

i18n.en: And the young woman was very fair to look upon, a virgin, and no man had known her; and she went down to the spring, and filled her jar, and came up.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֥רָץ הָעֶ֖בֶד לִקְרָאתָ֑הּ וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הַגְמִיאִ֥ינִי נָ֛א מְעַט־מַ֖יִם מִכַּדֵּֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me drink, I pray you, a little water from your jar.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֖אמֶר שְׁתֵ֣ה אֲדֹנִ֑י וַתְּמַהֵ֗ר וַתֹּ֧רֶד כַּדָּ֛הּ עַל־יָדָ֖הּ וַתַּשְׁקֵֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: And she said, Drink, my lord; and she hastened, and let down her jar upon her hand, and gave him drink.

paragraphs.text: וַתְּכַ֖ל לְהַשְׁקֹת֑וֹ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר גַּ֤ם לִגְמַלֶּ֙יךָ֙ אֶשְׁאָ֔ב עַ֥ד אִם־כִּלּ֖וּ לִשְׁתֹּֽת׃

i18n.en: And when she had finished giving him drink, she said, I will also draw for your camels, until they have finished drinking.

paragraphs.text: וַתְּמַהֵ֗ר וַתְּעַ֤ר כַּדָּהּ֙ אֶל־הַשֹּׁ֔קֶת וַתָּ֥רָץ ע֛וֹד אֶֽל־הַבְּאֵ֖ר לִשְׁאֹ֑ב וַתִּשְׁאַ֖ב לְכָל־גְּמַלָּֽיו׃

i18n.en: And she hastened, and emptied her jar into the trough, and ran again to the well to draw, and drew for all his camels.

paragraphs.text: וְהָאִ֥ישׁ מִשְׁתָּאֵ֖ה לָ֑הּ מַחֲרִ֕ישׁ לָדַ֗עַת הַֽהִצְלִ֧יחַ יְהוָ֛ה דַּרְכּ֖וֹ אִם־לֹֽא׃

i18n.en: And the man was gazing at her in silence, to know whether YHWH had prospered his journey or not.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר כִּלּ֤וּ הַגְּמַלִּים֙ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וַיִּקַּ֤ח הָאִישׁ֙ נֶ֣זֶם זָהָ֔ב בֶּ֖קַע מִשְׁקָל֑וֹ וּשְׁנֵ֤י צְמִידִים֙ עַל־יָדֶ֔יהָ עֲשָׂרָ֥ה זָהָ֖ב מִשְׁקָלָֽם׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when the camels had finished drinking, that the man took a golden nose-ring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold,

paragraphs.commentary:
The chapter's only weight-unit transaction. *Beqa* (half-shekel) is a rare HB lexeme — the only other clear occurrence is **Exod 38:26**, the half-shekel-per-head census-tax (*beqa la-gulgolet machatzit ha-shekel b-shekel ha-qodesh*), which explicitly identifies the *beqa* as *machatzit ha-shekel*. The standard-shekel mass is approximately 11.4 grams based on Iron Age weight-stone archaeology (Kletter 1998 *Economic Keystones*); inscribed weight-stones at Judahite sites preserve the *BQA* / *NTzP* / *PYM* unit-inventory. The HB economy operated by weighed bullion rather than by coinage until the Persian period.

The nose-ring + two bracelets total 20.5 shekels of gold ≈ 234 grams. In the betrothal-gift register, the weight-specification is formal-juridical content: the gift's value is recorded in weight-of-precious-metal because the gift is a quasi-contractual element of the marriage-negotiation (cf. Mesopotamian *terhatu*, Aramaic Elephantine marriage-contracts at TAD B2.6 / B3.8). The v 53 secondary gifts (silver vessels, gold vessels, garments, additional precious gifts to Lavan and the mother) escalate the value, but the v 22 initial gift establishes the formal opening of the negotiation.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ בַּת־מִ֣י אַ֔תְּ הַגִּ֥ידִי נָ֖א לִ֑י הֲיֵ֧שׁ בֵּית־אָבִ֛יךְ מָק֥וֹם לָ֖נוּ לָלִֽין׃

i18n.en: and said, Whose daughter are you? Tell me, I pray you. Is there room in your father's house for us to lodge?

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו בַּת־בְּתוּאֵ֖ל אָנֹ֑כִי בֶּן־מִלְכָּ֕ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָלְדָ֖ה לְנָחֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: And she said to him, I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milkah, whom she bore to Nachor.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו גַּם־תֶּ֥בֶן גַּם־מִסְפּ֖וֹא רַ֣ב עִמָּ֑נוּ גַּם־מָק֖וֹם לָלֽוּן׃

i18n.en: She said moreover to him, We have both straw and fodder in plenty, and room to lodge in.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקֹּ֣ד הָאִ֔ישׁ וַיִּשְׁתַּ֖חוּ לַֽיהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: And the man bowed his head, and prostrated himself before YHWH.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר בָּר֤וּךְ יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י אַבְרָהָ֔ם אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־עָזַ֥ב חַסְדּ֛וֹ וַאֲמִתּ֖וֹ מֵעִ֣ם אֲדֹנִ֑י אָנֹכִ֗י בַּדֶּ֙רֶךְ֙ נָחַ֣נִי יְהוָ֔ה בֵּ֖ית אֲחֵ֥י אֲדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he said, Blessed be YHWH, the Elohim of my master Avraham, who has not forsaken his chesed and his truth toward my master. As for me, YHWH has led me in the way to the house of my master's kin.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The first occurrence in the Hebrew Bible of the foundational virtue-pair *chesed v-emet* — *chesed and truth*.** The pair recurs at v 49 in the servant's appeal to Lavan and Bethuel, and across the patriarchal narratives at Gen 32:11 (Ya'aqov at the Jabbok) and Gen 47:29 (Ya'aqov to Yosef, paired with the oath-by-the-thigh). The canonical theological keystone is at **Exod 34:6** — the YHWH self-revelation at Sinai after the Golden Calf — where YHWH proclaims his attributes with *rav-chesed v-emet* at the structural center. The Gen 24:27 prayer thus addresses YHWH in the very terms YHWH will use to self-reveal at Sinai; the structural-thematic anticipation is editorially deliberate.

The lexeme *chesed* is preserved untranslated per established WoH policy on theologically-loaded terms with no single English equivalent. The standard English renderings — KJV *lovingkindness* (Coverdale's neologism), ASV *mercy* (narrower than the Hebrew), NRSV *steadfast love* (capturing only the loyal-love dimension), NJPS *kindness* — all flatten the lexeme's semantic core: loyal action toward a covenantal partner, gracious action exceeding what is owed, the disposition that grounds both. **Sakenfeld** *The Meaning of Hesed in the Hebrew Bible* (HSM 17, 1978) refines **Glueck's** foundational *Das Wort Hesed* (1927): chesed is the action of a more-powerful party on behalf of a less-powerful party in an established relationship, where the more-powerful party could have declined to act. **Clark** *The Word Hesed in the Hebrew Bible* (JSOTSup 157, 1993) extends the corpus-comprehensive analysis. The Sakenfeld refinement is the modern critical consensus.

The pair's cross-corpus reach is among the most extensive in the HB: Gen 24:27, 24:49, 32:11, 47:29; Exod 34:6; Josh 2:14; 2 Sam 2:6, 15:20; Ps 25:10, 40:11-12, 57:4, 61:8, 85:11, 86:15, 89:15, 138:2; Prov 3:3, 14:22, 16:6, 20:28; Hos 4:1; Mic 7:20. Twenty-plus principal occurrences across the canon.

paragraphs.text: וַתָּ֙רָץ֙ הַֽנַּעֲרָ֔ וַתַּגֵּ֖ד לְבֵ֣ית אִמָּ֑הּ כַּדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵֽלֶּה׃

i18n.en: And the young woman ran, and told her mother's house according to these words.

paragraphs.text: וּלְרִבְקָ֥ה אָ֖ח וּשְׁמ֣וֹ לָבָ֑ן וַיָּ֨רָץ לָבָ֧ן אֶל־הָאִ֛ישׁ הַח֖וּצָה אֶל־הָעָֽיִן׃

i18n.en: And Rivkah had a brother, and his name was Lavan; and Lavan ran out to the man, to the spring.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י ׀ כִּרְאֹ֣ת אֶת־הַנֶּ֗זֶם וְֽאֶת־הַצְּמִדִים֮ עַל־יְדֵ֣י אֲחֹתוֹ֒ וּכְשָׁמְע֗וֹ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֞י רִבְקָ֤ה אֲחֹתוֹ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר כֹּֽה־דִבֶּ֥ר אֵלַ֖י הָאִ֑ישׁ וַיָּבֹא֙ אֶל־הָאִ֔ישׁ וְהִנֵּ֛ה עֹמֵ֥ד עַל־הַגְּמַלִּ֖ים עַל־הָעָֽיִן׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when he saw the nose-ring, and the bracelets upon his sister's hands, and when he heard the words of Rivkah his sister, saying, Thus the man spoke to me — that he came to the man; and behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בּ֖וֹא בְּר֣וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה לָ֤מָּה תַעֲמֹד֙ בַּח֔וּץ וְאָנֹכִי֙ פִּנִּ֣יתִי הַבַּ֔יִת וּמָק֖וֹם לַגְּמַלִּֽים׃

i18n.en: And he said, Come in, you blessed of YHWH; why do you stand outside? For I have prepared the house, and a place for the camels.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֤א הָאִישׁ֙ הַבַּ֔יְתָה וַיְפַתַּ֖ח הַגְּמַלִּ֑ים וַיִּתֵּ֨ן תֶּ֤בֶן וּמִסְפּוֹא֙ לַגְּמַלִּ֔ים וּמַ֙יִם֙ לִרְחֹ֣ץ רַגְלָ֔יו וְרַגְלֵ֥י הָאֲנָשִׁ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And the man came into the house, and he unloaded the camels; and he gave straw and fodder for the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him.

paragraphs.text: ויישם [וַיּוּשַׂ֤ם] לְפָנָיו֙ לֶאֱכֹ֔ל וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ לֹ֣א אֹכַ֔ל עַ֥ד אִם־דִּבַּ֖רְתִּי דְּבָרָ֑י וַיֹּ֖אמֶר דַּבֵּֽר׃

i18n.en: And there was set before him food to eat; but he said, I will not eat until I have spoken my errand. And he said, Speak on.

paragraphs.commentary: Ketiv/qere variant. The ketiv ויישם (*vayisem* / *vayyisam* — vague pointing, possibly a corrupted hophal or qal form) is replaced by the qere וַיּוּשַׂם (*vayyusam* — clear hophal: *and-it-was-set*). The WoH translation follows the qere per standard MT practice, matching ASV's *And there was set*. The variant is the chapter's only ketiv/qere divergence.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמַ֑ר עֶ֥בֶד אַבְרָהָ֖ם אָנֹֽכִי׃

i18n.en: And he said, I am Avraham's servant.

paragraphs.text: וַיהוָ֞ה בֵּרַ֧ךְ אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֛י מְאֹ֖ד וַיִּגְדָּ֑ל וַיִּתֶּן־ל֞וֹ צֹ֤אן וּבָקָר֙ וְכֶ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֔ב וַעֲבָדִם֙ וּשְׁפָחֹ֔ת וּגְמַלִּ֖ים וַחֲמֹרִֽים׃

i18n.en: And YHWH has blessed my master greatly, and he is become great; and he has given him flocks and herds, and silver and gold, and male and female slaves, and camels and donkeys.

paragraphs.text: וַתֵּ֡לֶד שָׂרָה֩ אֵ֨שֶׁת אֲדֹנִ֥י בֵן֙ לַֽאדֹנִ֔י אַחֲרֵ֖י זִקְנָתָ֑הּ וַיִּתֶּן־לּ֖וֹ אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־לֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Sarah my master's wife bore a son to my master when she was old; and to him he has given all that he has.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשְׁבִּעֵ֥נִי אֲדֹנִ֖י לֵאמֹ֑ר לֹא־תִקַּ֤ח אִשָּׁה֙ לִבְנִ֔י מִבְּנוֹת֙ הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּאַרְצֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And my master made me swear, saying, You shall not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Kena'ani, in whose land I dwell;

paragraphs.text: אִם־לֹ֧א אֶל־בֵּית־אָבִ֛י תֵּלֵ֖ךְ וְאֶל־מִשְׁפַּחְתִּ֑י וְלָקַחְתָּ֥ אִשָּׁ֖ה לִבְנִֽי׃

i18n.en: but you shall go to my father's house, and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son.

paragraphs.text: וָאֹמַ֖ר אֶל־אֲדֹנִ֑י אֻלַ֛י לֹא־תֵלֵ֥ךְ הָאִשָּׁ֖ה אַחֲרָֽי׃

i18n.en: And I said to my master, Perhaps the woman will not follow me.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֵלָ֑י יְהוָ֞ה אֲשֶׁר־הִתְהַלַּ֣כְתִּי לְפָנָ֗יו יִשְׁלַ֨ח מַלְאָכ֤וֹ אִתָּךְ֙ וְהִצְלִ֣יחַ דַּרְכֶּ֔ךָ וְלָקַחְתָּ֤ אִשָּׁה֙ לִבְנִ֔י מִמִּשְׁפַּחְתִּ֖י וּמִבֵּ֥ית אָבִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he said to me, YHWH, before whom I have walked, will send his messenger with you, and prosper your way; and you shall take a wife for my son of my kindred, and of my father's house.

paragraphs.text: אָ֤ז תִּנָּקֶה֙ מֵאָ֣לָתִ֔י כִּ֥י תָב֖וֹא אֶל־מִשְׁפַּחְתִּ֑י וְאִם־לֹ֤א יִתְּנוּ֙ לָ֔ךְ וְהָיִ֥יתָ נָקִ֖י מֵאָלָתִֽי׃

i18n.en: Then you shall be clear from my oath, when you come to my kindred; and if they will not give her to you, you shall be clear from my oath.

paragraphs.text: וָאָבֹ֥א הַיּ֖וֹם אֶל־הָעָ֑יִן וָאֹמַ֗ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י אַבְרָהָ֔ם אִם־יֶשְׁךָ־נָּא֙ מַצְלִ֣יחַ דַּרְכִּ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י הֹלֵ֥ךְ עָלֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And I came this day to the spring, and said, YHWH, the Elohim of my master Avraham, if now you do prosper my way which I go,

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּ֛ה אָנֹכִ֥י נִצָּ֖ב עַל־עֵ֣ין הַמָּ֑יִם וְהָיָ֤ה הָֽעַלְמָה֙ הַיֹּצֵ֣את לִשְׁאֹ֔ב וְאָמַרְתִּ֣י אֵלֶ֔יהָ הַשְׁקִֽינִי־נָ֥א מְעַט־מַ֖יִם מִכַּדֵּֽךְ׃

i18n.en: Behold, I am standing by the spring of water; and let it come to pass that the maiden who comes out to draw, to whom I shall say, Give me, I pray you, a little water from your jar to drink,

paragraphs.text: וְאָמְרָ֤ה אֵלַי֙ גַּם־אַתָּ֣ה שְׁתֵ֔ה וְגַ֥ם לִגְמַלֶּ֖יךָ אֶשְׁאָ֑ב הִ֣וא הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־הֹכִ֥יחַ יְהוָ֖ה לְבֶן־אֲדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: and she shall say to me, Drink, you also, and I will also draw for your camels — let her be the woman whom YHWH has appointed for my master's son.

paragraphs.text: אֲנִי֩ טֶ֨רֶם אֲכַלֶּ֜ה לְדַבֵּ֣ר אֶל־לִבִּ֗י וְהִנֵּ֨ה רִבְקָ֤ה יֹצֵאת֙ וְכַדָּ֣הּ עַל־שִׁכְמָ֔הּ וַתֵּ֥רֶד הָעַ֖יְנָה וַתִּשְׁאָ֑ב וָאֹמַ֥ר אֵלֶ֖יהָ הַשְׁקִ֥ינִי נָֽא׃

i18n.en: Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rivkah came out, with her jar on her shoulder; and she went down to the spring, and drew. And I said to her, Let me drink, I pray you.

paragraphs.text: וַתְּמַהֵ֗ר וַתּ֤וֹרֶד כַּדָּהּ֙ מֵֽעָלֶ֔יהָ וַתֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁתֵ֔ה וְגַם־גְּמַלֶּ֖יךָ אַשְׁקֶ֑ה וָאֵ֕שְׁתְּ וְגַ֥ם הַגְּמַלִּ֖ים הִשְׁקָֽתָה׃

i18n.en: And she hastened, and let down her jar from her shoulder, and said, Drink, and I will give your camels drink also; so I drank, and she made the camels drink also.

paragraphs.text: וָאֶשְׁאַ֣ל אֹתָ֗הּ וָאֹמַר֮ בַּת־מִ֣י אַתְּ֒ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר בַּת־בְּתוּאֵל֙ בֶּן־נָח֔וֹר אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָֽלְדָה־לּ֖וֹ מִלְכָּ֑ה וָאָשִׂ֤ם הַנֶּ֙זֶם֙ עַל־אַפָּ֔הּ וְהַצְּמִידִ֖ים עַל־יָדֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter are you? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nachor's son, whom Milkah bore to him. And I put the nose-ring upon her nose, and the bracelets upon her hands.

paragraphs.text: וָאֶקֹּ֥ד וָֽאֶשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֖ה לַיהוָ֑ה וָאֲבָרֵ֗ךְ אֶת־יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י אַבְרָהָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֤ר הִנְחַ֙נִי֙ בְּדֶ֣רֶךְ אֱמֶ֔ת לָקַ֛חַת אֶת־בַּת־אֲחִ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖י לִבְנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And I bowed my head, and prostrated myself before YHWH, and blessed YHWH, the Elohim of my master Avraham, who had led me in the right way to take my master's brother's daughter for his son.

paragraphs.text: וְ֠עַתָּה אִם־יֶשְׁכֶ֨ם עֹשִׂ֜ים חֶ֧סֶד וֶֽאֱמֶ֛ת אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖י הַגִּ֣ידוּ לִ֑י וְאִם־לֹ֕א הַגִּ֣ידוּ לִ֔י וְאֶפְנֶ֥ה עַל־יָמִ֖ין א֥וֹ עַל־שְׂמֹֽאל׃

i18n.en: And now if you will show chesed and truth to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֨עַן לָבָ֤ן וּבְתוּאֵל֙ וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ מֵיְהוָ֖ה יָצָ֣א הַדָּבָ֑ר לֹ֥א נוּכַ֛ל דַּבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖יךָ רַ֥ע אוֹ־טֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: Then Lavan and Bethuel answered and said, The matter has come forth from YHWH; we cannot speak to you bad or good.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Me-YHWH yatza ha-davar* — *the matter has come forth from YHWH* — is a divine-providence-acknowledgement formula. The family's role is reduced from active-choosing to ratification of an already-decreed outcome. The closest constructional parallel is **Isa 45:23** (*bi nishbati yatza mi-pi tzedakah davar v-lo yashuv* — *by myself I have sworn; the word has gone forth from my mouth in righteousness and shall not return*), where the verb *yatza* + *davar* governs a divine speech-act. The HB pattern of *non-Israelite-or-wavering-figure acknowledges YHWH's sovereignty over an outcome they cannot resist* recurs at Gen 31:24 (Lavan's later dream-warning), Gen 41:38-39 (Pharaoh to Yosef), Num 23-24 (Balaam), Josh 2:9-11 (Rachav), 1 Sam 24:17-20 (Saul), Dan 2-6 (Nebuchadnezzar and Darius). Lavan and Bethuel's response is the patriarchal inaugural instance.

The Lavan-before-Bethuel order is editorially significant. **Sarna** (*JPS* p. 167) reads it as evidence of Lavan's primacy in the household-economy, comparing the **Nuzi marriage-contracts** (HSS V, JEN, AASOR 16) in which the bride's brother appears as the agnate-protector and the principal-agent in the marriage negotiation while the father plays a secondary role. The Nuzi parallels were extensively developed in mid-twentieth-century scholarship (Speiser 1955; Gordon 1937) and have been critically reviewed since (Greengus 1975 *JAOS* 95; Eichler 1989 *JANES* 18); the brother-as-agnate-protector reading remains defensible. An alternative critical reading (Westermann p. 387) treats the *u-Bethuel* as a textual interpolation, the v 50 response originally Lavan-only — Bethuel disappears from the chapter after this verse (vv 53, 55 name Lavan and the mother). The closing merism *lo nukhal daber elekha ra o-tov* — *we cannot speak to you bad or good* — is Lavan's idiom, recurring at Gen 31:24, 29 and at Num 24:13.

paragraphs.text: הִנֵּֽה־רִבְקָ֥ה לְפָנֶ֖יךָ קַ֣ח וָלֵ֑ךְ וּתְהִ֤י אִשָּׁה֙ לְבֶן־אֲדֹנֶ֔יךָ כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: Behold, Rivkah is before you; take her, and go, and let her be your master's son's wife, as YHWH has spoken.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁמַ֛ע עֶ֥בֶד אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֶת־דִּבְרֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּשְׁתַּ֥חוּ אַ֖רְצָה לַֽיהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when Avraham's servant heard their words, that he prostrated himself to the ground before YHWH.

paragraphs.text: וַיּוֹצֵ֨א הָעֶ֜בֶד כְּלֵי־כֶ֨סֶף וּכְלֵ֤י זָהָב֙ וּבְגָדִ֔ים וַיִּתֵּ֖ן לְרִבְקָ֑ה וּמִ֨גְדָּנֹ֔ת נָתַ֥ן לְאָחִ֖יהָ וּלְאִמָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: And the servant brought out vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rivkah; he also gave precious gifts to her brother and to her mother.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאכְל֣וּ וַיִּשְׁתּ֗וּ ה֛וּא וְהָאֲנָשִׁ֥ים אֲשֶׁר־עִמּ֖וֹ וַיָּלִ֑ינוּ וַיָּק֣וּמוּ בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֹּ֖אמֶר שַׁלְּחֻ֥נִי לַֽאדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And they ate and drank, he and the men who were with him, and lodged there. And they rose up in the morning, and he said, Send me away to my master.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אָחִ֙יהָ֙ וְאִמָּ֔הּ תֵּשֵׁ֨ב הַנַּעֲרָ֥ אִתָּ֛נוּ יָמִ֖ים א֣וֹ עָשׂ֑וֹר אַחַ֖ר תֵּלֵֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And her brother and her mother said, Let the young woman stay with us a few days, at least ten; after that she shall go.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵהֶם֙ אַל־תְּאַחֲר֣וּ אֹתִ֔י וַֽיהוָ֖ה הִצְלִ֣יחַ דַּרְכִּ֑י שַׁלְּח֕וּנִי וְאֵלְכָ֖ה לַֽאדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he said to them, Do not delay me, since YHWH has prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ נִקְרָ֣א לַֽנַּעֲרָ֑ וְנִשְׁאֲלָ֖ה אֶת־פִּֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And they said, We will call the young woman, and ask her own mouth.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרְא֤וּ לְרִבְקָה֙ וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלֶ֔יהָ הֲתֵלְכִ֖י עִם־הָאִ֣ישׁ הַזֶּ֑ה וַתֹּ֖אמֶר אֵלֵֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And they called Rivkah, and said to her, Will you go with this man? And she said, I will go.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְשַׁלְּח֛וּ אֶת־רִבְקָ֥ה אֲחֹתָ֖ם וְאֶת־מֵנִקְתָּ֑הּ וְאֶת־עֶ֥בֶד אַבְרָהָ֖ם וְאֶת־אֲנָשָֽׁיו׃

i18n.en: And they sent away Rivkah their sister, and her nurse, and Avraham's servant, and his men.

paragraphs.text: וַיְבָרֲכ֤וּ אֶת־רִבְקָה֙ וַיֹּ֣אמְרוּ לָ֔הּ אֲחֹתֵ֕נוּ אַ֥תְּ הֲיִ֖י לְאַלְפֵ֣י רְבָבָ֑ה וְיִירַ֣שׁ זַרְעֵ֔ךְ אֵ֖ת שַׁ֥עַר שֹׂנְאָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And they blessed Rivkah, and said to her, Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your seed possess the gate of those who hate them.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The matriarchal-fertility blessing-formula** — *achotenu at hayi l-alfei revavah v-yiyrash zar'ekh et sha'ar son'av* — and the chapter's most editorially-deliberate cross-reference to Gen 22:17. The second half of the verse (*v-yiyrash zar'ekh et sha'ar son'av*) verbally echoes Avraham's blessing at the *aqedah*: *v-yiyrash zar'akha et sha'ar oyvav* — *may your seed possess the gate of his enemies* — with the pronoun shifted from masculine (Avraham's seed) to feminine (Rivkah's seed). The verbal echo establishes a structural inclusio across the Abraham cycle: the bride enters the patriarchal family under a blessing that mirrors the patriarch's own foundational blessing.

The formula is the **canonical matriarchal counterpart to the patriarchal-seed-comparison-triad** (dust at Gen 13:16, stars at 15:5, sand at 22:17; see *patriarchal-seed-comparison-triad*). The masculine-patriarchal formulae use cosmographic-natural similes (dust, stars, sand); the matriarchal formula uses a numerical-arithmetic expression (*alfei revavah* — *thousands of ten-thousands*, equivalent to *myriads of myriads* / *millions*). The lexical distinction is editorially meaningful but the theological function is parallel. **Trible** (*God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality* 1978 pp. 27-31) reads the distinction as part of the HB's broader gendered-blessing rhetoric: masculine-patriarchal blessings frame in terms of cosmographic-spatial extension; matriarchal blessings frame in terms of numerical-generational descent.

The formula's matriarchal-canonical status is confirmed at **Ruth 4:11-12** — the marriage of Boaz and Ruth — where the elders and people at the gate of Bethlehem bless Ruth with the explicit invocation of the matriarchs (*k-Rachel u-k-Le'ah asher banu sh'tehem et-bet Yisrael*) and extend the formula to Tamar (*v-yhi vetkha k-veit-Peretz asher yaledah Tamar l-Yehudah*), completing the four-matriarch + Tamar tableau that underwrites the Davidic genealogy. The Ruth recurrence is the canonical confirmation of the matriarchal-blessing as a HB literary form.

paragraphs.text: וַתָּ֨קָם רִבְקָ֜ה וְנַעֲרֹתֶ֗יהָ וַתִּרְכַּ֙בְנָה֙ עַל־הַגְּמַלִּ֔ים וַתֵּלַ֖כְנָה אַחֲרֵ֣י הָאִ֑ישׁ וַיִּקַּ֥ח הָעֶ֛בֶד אֶת־רִבְקָ֖ה וַיֵּלַֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And Rivkah arose with her maidens, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man; and the servant took Rivkah, and went his way.

paragraphs.text: וְיִצְחָק֙ בָּ֣א מִבּ֔וֹא בְּאֵ֥ר לַחַ֖י רֹאִ֑י וְה֥וּא יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּאֶ֥רֶץ הַנֶּֽגֶב׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq had come from the way of Be'er Lachai Ro'i; for he dwelt in the land of the Negev.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּצֵ֥א יִצְחָ֛ק לָשׂ֥וּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶ֖ה לִפְנ֣וֹת עָ֑רֶב וַיִּשָּׂ֤א עֵינָיו֙ וַיַּ֔רְא וְהִנֵּ֥ה גְמַלִּ֖ים בָּאִֽים׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq went out to meditate in the field at the turning of evening; and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and behold, there were camels coming.

paragraphs.commentary:
*La-suach* is a HB hapax legomenon (qal infinitive of an uncertain root *s-w-ch* or *s-y-ch*) and one of the most-discussed lexical cruxes in the chapter. **Six readings** circulate across the ancient versions, the rabbinic tradition, and modern philology:

1. **'to meditate'** — Vulgate *ad meditandum*, ASV/KJV/ESV; the *siach* (meditation) cognate. Default modern-English-traditional.
2. **'to converse / chatter / occupy oneself in thought'** — LXX *adoleschēsai*; the *siach* (speech, talk) cognate.
3. **'to pray'** — Targum Onkelos (*l-tzala'ah*), Rashi. **The rabbinic-canonical reading:** *b. Berakhot 26b* reads the verse as the institution of the afternoon *Minchah* prayer-service — *Yitzchaq tiken tefillat minchah* — paired with Avraham instituting *Shacharit* (from Gen 19:27) and Ya'aqov instituting *Ma'ariv* (from Gen 28:11). The three-times-daily prayer-cycle's patriarchal-etiology rests on this verse.
4. **'to commune / converse'** — Speiser *AB Genesis*, some modern English.
5. **'to complain / lament'** — minority modern philological, connecting *suach* to *siach* in its lament-register (Ps 55:3, 64:2). Would frame Yitzchaq's evening-activity as continued mourning for Sarah (cf. v 67 *va-yinacheim Yitzchaq acharei imo*).
6. **'to wander / walk about'** — NRSV; modern philological treatment relating *suach* to *sh-w-ch* (with Akkadian and Aramaic cognates).

The WoH translation renders *la-suach* as *to meditate* — the ASV/Vulgate default, preserving the contemplative register closest to the *siach*-cluster semantic field, neutral on the meditate-vs.-pray-vs.-wander question. The rabbinic-canonical Minchah-institution reading is not preempted: the choice of *meditate* is editorially-conservative on the hapax, and the apparatus carries the six-reading documentation. The verse pairs with the *sa-eynekha* lift-your-eyes formula at the same verse (*va-yisa eynav va-yar* — *he lifted up his eyes and saw*) — the formula recurs at v 64 in Rivkah's parallel-action.

paragraphs.text: וַתִּשָּׂ֤א רִבְקָה֙ אֶת־עֵינֶ֔יהָ וַתֵּ֖רֶא אֶת־יִצְחָ֑ק וַתִּפֹּ֖ל מֵעַ֥ל הַגָּמָֽל׃

i18n.en: And Rivkah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Yitzchaq, she alighted from the camel.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־הָעֶ֗בֶד מִֽי־הָאִ֤ישׁ הַלָּזֶה֙ הַהֹלֵ֤ךְ בַּשָּׂדֶה֙ לִקְרָאתֵ֔נוּ וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הָעֶ֖בֶד ה֣וּא אֲדֹנִ֑י וַתִּקַּ֥ח הַצָּעִ֖יף וַתִּתְכָּֽס׃

i18n.en: And she said to the servant, Who is that man walking in the field to meet us? And the servant said, It is my master. And she took her veil, and covered herself.

paragraphs.text: וַיְסַפֵּ֥ר הָעֶ֖בֶד לְיִצְחָ֑ק אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָֽׂה׃

i18n.en: And the servant told Yitzchaq all the things that he had done.

paragraphs.text: וַיְבִאֶ֣הָ יִצְחָ֗ק הָאֹ֙הֱלָה֙ שָׂרָ֣ה אִמּ֔וֹ וַיִּקַּ֧ח אֶת־רִבְקָ֛ה וַתְּהִי־ל֥וֹ לְאִשָּׁ֖ה וַיֶּאֱהָבֶ֑הָ וַיִּנָּחֵ֥ם יִצְחָ֖ק אַחֲרֵ֥י אִמּֽוֹ׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother, and took Rivkah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. And Yitzchaq was comforted after his mother.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The Sarah-to-Rivkah generational-transition formula** closes the chapter and the Abraham cycle's marriage-and-burial sequence. Sarah's death at Gen 23 sets up Rivkah's arrival at Gen 24:67: she enters the tent of Sarah his mother (*ha-ohelah Sarah imo*), the literal-locational succession from one matriarch to the next. The nifal *va-yinacheim* (*was comforted*) — from *n-ch-m* — is the HB's standard consolation-formula, recurring at major mourning-moments: Gen 37:35 (Ya'aqov refusing to be comforted for Yosef); 2 Sam 13:39 (David comforted for Amnon); Isa 40:1 (*nachamu nachamu ami* — the inaugural verse of Second Isaiah).

Avraham himself does not appear as an actor in the rest of the cycle: Gen 25:1-11 narrates his second marriage (to Keturah) and his death in summary. The chapter thus closes the Abraham cycle proper. The structural triptych of the cycle's closing — the *aqedah* at Gen 22, the death of Sarah at Gen 23, the bride-quest at Gen 24 — pairs the binding of the seed-child, the burial of the matriarch, and the arrival of the next matriarch as three movements of a single closing sequence.
